claims.text: The proposed framework independently models lattice and electronic thermal transport through anharmonic phonon scattering and electron–phonon interactions.
Separating lattice and electronic transport will produce more accurate total thermal-conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr.
The new approach will reduce prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional Debye- or DFT-based models.
The target material is high-purity, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with minimal defects and oxygen.
The approach does not rely on an averaged parameter such as a single Debye temperature.
The approach is applicable from below 200 K to 1200 K.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions arising from variations in atomic mass and force constants govern phonon dynamics.
Intrinsic electronic states act alongside lattice distortions as a mediator of heat transport.
Anharmonic phonon scattering and electron–phonon interactions have distinct temperature dependences that should be modeled separately.
The lattice thermal-conductivity contribution in HfNbTaTiZr remains nearly constant from 300 to 1200 K.
The lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are nearly equal below 200 K.
The predicted total thermal conductivity will fall within approximately 10–17 W/(K·m).
Electronic thermal conductivity has a stronger temperature dependence than lattice thermal conductivity and becomes relatively more significant below 200 K.
Previous models based on averaged elastic properties or a single Debye temperature conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Previous models have higher prediction errors and cannot capture the distinct temperature dependences of lattice and electronic heat transport.
Significant impurities, structural defects, or secondary phases alter scattering mechanisms and limit the approach's accuracy.
Electrical resistivity combined with the Wiedemann–Franz law can be used to estimate the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
A deviation greater than approximately 30% between predicted and measured total conductivity across the stated temperature range falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to observe near-equal lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K or a nearly constant lattice contribution from 300 to 1200 K falsifies the hypothesis.
